It’s interesting that Boris Tadić, the former president of Serbia (part of the previous regime, who lost to Vučić 14 years ago) echoes the same type of pronouncements about politicians and the commenters here on HN, and I do not mean this in a particularly laudatory sense. Just recently he was sending messages about how political experience, political vision and the like are key. How to be a political leader one needs this or that, or how Serbia requires this or that type of engagement with future technologies to remain relevant, comparing the student movement to blockchain (yes, really). This (incredibly vain and pompous) man doubtlessly has the most political experience in Serbia right now, and sits in several boards of Chinese and other multinationals, with other consulting roles, pretty much proving the bankability of his political talents. And yet that’s the person behind a series of political decisions and circumstances which inaugurated the previous regime. Also, looking around the globe at professional politicians once also lauded for their political talent, like Macron, or Merkel, I’m really not seeing their policies paying off in spades, nor their "political vision" proving particularly beneficial to their citizenry at the moment. In all three cases, it seems, seasoned politicians made capital errors in judgement which are now causing resentment, almost unprecedented political realignments and upheaval across these nations. People are incredibly quick to judge the potential behaviour of a future political formation - yet Western democracies are by and large falling apart, as a result of career politicians’ actions, inactions, stupidity and avarice? As people speak more and more loudly on certain issues, like Palestine, these same politicians are comfortable ignoring them. Where is the scepticism for them, or the viability of this guild-like way of structuring the political sphere as the way forward? We are living the consequences of having career politicians lead, do we like it so much we cannot conceive of anything better? Anyway, if you look into the local press in Serbia and especially enclaves like Twitter, there’s a wonderful symmetry: the EU champions are terrified the student movement has already shown "concerning" right leanings, they’re busy counting how many EU flags the students have draped themselves in while marching, and aren’t happy. The right is deeply worried about how the "globalist, NGO, pro-EU camarilla" is already deeply embedded in the student movement (they went to Brussels, after all!) and is perhaps even planting their candidates into the mix to sell out the country’s interests to the globalists. I am being slightly ironic here, but I have nothing but contempt for this thinking on both sides. Winning the election required the participation and support from both these camps’ voting blocks, which tells you how bad the situation truly was, since sworn enemies were forced to cooperate with a political unknown just for the chance to win against the existing political regime. In a sense, only a political unknown could have won, as all pre-existing political factions, (mostly comprised of these praised seasoned politicians, many of them three decades into their careers) would not or could not muster the strength or wherewithal to work with one another. No nationalist would ever cooperate with a globalist pro-EU green party, even if it cost them their country, democracy, and those same national interests they hold sacrosanct. Likewise, no progressive citizen party saving democratic principles would ever work with what they view as backward retrograde nationalist movements threatening to plunge the country back into the type of rhetoric and milieu as existed during the wars of the nineties. Also, at some point the decades-long careers of many politicians was perfect cannon fodder for the regime’s propaganda machine, gleefully cataloguing their past sins and outright inventing them if the need arose. After a while, political experience morphs into evidence of one’s political parasitism. It took a decentralised student movement which could not be targeted and besmirched, to engage the non-voting public and voters on both sides of the political spectrum. Part of the reason why all parties which took part in this election were swept away (except for the students and the outgoing regime) was because of failing to recognise the political moment. This election, in my view, was a single-issue election - the workings of democracy and stopping corruption and the further decay of institutions. This is what the political movement will be judged on, and what will determine its political future. The citizenry, at this juncture, is willing to table discussions on foreign policy for the sake of internal affairs and weeding out corruption. Most foreign powers and press corps, sadly, are interested primarily in the foreign policy implications of this new movement, and seem like they couldn’t care less if Serbian citizenry lives in caves, favelas, or in a thriving democracy. Many things are still unclear, such as the exact relationship between the Parliament and Government, once formed, and the direct democracy practiced by the student movement. It is unclear how effective it will prove, or how they will select their allies and collaborators, as it’s perfectly obvious that the movement cannot simply replace the totality of public administration. Regardless, the new regime will enjoy a broad latitude and a measure of good will among the citizenry not seen in a generation. It needs to use that to good effect. If it fails to deliver, they will be ridiculed and attacked by members of both internal factions, and will more than likely splinter, and usher in a return of Vučić, who - lest we forget - is now the only opposition party in Parliament, with a sizeable number of representatives, and plenty of corrosive residuals and slush funds and media operations still at his disposal. Lest we also forget, with 700k party members, it is a powerful organisation even without the corruptive backend of the state apparatus.

It's an incredibly messy space and the particulars are going to vary wildly based on the company. A company in a more regulated space may have the finances to standardize on Siemens or something similarly fancy, but smaller manufacturers may not have any standard at all and you'll be looking at a mix of Rockwell, Allen-Bradley, Honeywell and even more niche brands and PLCs. Many vendors have "proprietary" languages, but they're all going to be very basic stuff that is essentially Visual Basic, C, or JavaScript-ish. It's not going to be a formal software development environment like you're used to. In less regulated environments, a lot of the time you'll find that the PLC/automation component is being handled by the MAINTENANCE or FACILITIES people. So for an example of a problem I'm facing, we have some Vacuum Furnaces. Essentially before you can turn titanium into a useful implant, you have to bake titanium at a temperature above its ignition point so that the molecules can loosen up enough and release the stresses that accumulate in the forging process. As part of this process, there's eight thermocouples of different sensitivities and at least three pressure/vacuum sensors all physically wired into a "chart recorder". The thermocouple "data" is literally a voltage reading, and the chart recorder is interpreting that and converting it into an integer and storing that in RAM. These devices are about 20 years old, and it can only hold about 24 hours of data, so you have to network it with a server that can store those readings in case you ever need to prove to someone that this step of your process was done right. It's not technically complex, but these devices aren't easy to interact with and often require physically connecting to them to make changes. There's all sorts of possibilities for really meaningful integrations with other manufacturing systems, ERP systems, data analysis and visualization, and basically a million "low hanging fruit" problems in the space that simply don't get done because don't have enough people with any technical skill at all. Most companies I've worked for literally don't care about what the solution is, so you get a ton of leeway on architecting the solution. IMO, the best part is that it feels like you're accomplishing something. Making a real impact. You can walk the floor and see the code you wrote building things. Doing things. You know the engineer who came to you with a problem, and you delivered a solution that makes his life easier. Not to make some abstract number go up for a quarterly report, but to actually make things that are useful.

Hi HN, kc is a Kotlin compiler for the JVM, written in Go. Why I built it: most Kotlin tools, like linters, KSP and the language server, are built on kotlinc's frontend, so they're only as fast as it is. A fast frontend could make room for: - Linters that run in milliseconds instead of seconds - A fast language server - Much faster KSP annotation processing - Quicker builds in CI, where every run starts a cold JVM - Fast feedback for coding agents, which compile and fix code in a loop many times per task I measured big gains in both speed and memory against kotlinc 2.4.21, running warm as in the Gradle daemon: - kotlinx-coroutines-core: 2.50 s → 159 ms (16x) - Ktor core modules: 2.32 s → 226 ms (10x) - kotlinpoet: 1.23 s → 97 ms (13x) - Memory: ~1 GB → ~100 MB What it doesn't do yet: - A few language features aren't supported - No warnings, and only the errors that type checking finds, so some invalid code compiles - JVM only, no Gradle plugin or IDE support - Passes 95% of kotlinc's box tests It's a prototype, but I plan to keep working on it until it's useful for a wide range of real projects. Benchmark details and how to repeat them:  https://github.com/barteo/kotlin-compiler-go/blob/main/docs/...

I write a spec by speaking, not much thought given to grammar and sentence structure.  I over-describe concepts, over-describe functionality.  A lot of repetition of details and concepts.  The audience is not a human.  Whisper converts it to text. Lightly manually edit for speech rec failures. LLM takes that and converts it into a much much denser, much more structured technical spec in markdown.  This is issue 1 in the repo. I edit this directly extensively, adding detail, removing misconceptions, adding sections with more dictated text. LLM takes this and further densifies it, closer to an actual implementor’s spec.  I carefully note what got added, removed, edited in this step. I edit this carefully and extensively again. Some removals get added back, some additions get removed.  This is the first commit and closes issue 1. I then have an LLM write an implementation plan and basic project scaffolding.  Makefiles, smoke tests, logging, test framework, DI. I edit the plan, and the plan is the second commit.  An LLM uses both plus scaffolding plus my repo policy documents (global) to write a README.  We’re still single threaded. An agent files the first n top level implementation tickets.  These refer to and sometimes quote any interface contracts in the spec or implementation plan.  These usually map 1-to-1 to a module/directory.  These sometimes have stub commits to create the module directory and commit interface definitions.  Some larger modules have a README in their module directory if their purpose or structure or inputs or outputs are complicated or non-obvious. Parallel agents write commit level issues that are the task items for each top level implementation ticket.  One agent per module. Then, spawn parallel agents with detailed global instructions, the full spec+plan, and the full readme, and the full code from the module it is working in, plus the issue text.  Its output is a single commit on the feature branch and a PR that closes out one feature ticket. This spawns an adversarial reviewer which has detailed agent instructions as well as our code style guides and repo policies.  The scaffolding includes tests and linting and checks. Any failures spawn rework agents until the feature branch is up to snuff. I review the feature branch diff and merge it, having read the review and rework comments on the PR.  I frequently add comments about the implementation (“don’t do x, do y”) and add WIP: back to loop it back for more rework.  I don’t see anything that isn’t green, formatted, passes linting, passes tests, and a (dumb) bot thinks is ready to land.  Most of the time, it is.  Sometimes, it did it the wrong way and I correct it. The more modular the code, the easier it is to parallelize (obviously).  It is ridiculously easy to build large software quickly now, provided it is sufficiently modular so the implementation doesn’t have to cross modules very much.  The detailed spec and implementation plan up front helps a lot with this.  It’s a lot like writing multithreaded programs really. Any bugs discovered are tackled with strict TDD, one commit with a failing test, one bugfix commit that must be green and not touch the test. Individual modules must conform to good contracts, meet best OOP practices, and fit into context.  Too big and they get broken down further.  Context size is actually a useful constraint for code structure here. This workflow, the code standards, the styleguide, the linter settings, the fmt settings (obviously only applicable to non-Go as the Go fmt is not configurable), everything is global and stored in another repo and is vendored into each AI managed project repo.  It has a fair bit of “I shouldn’t have to say this, but…” stuff (in the style of “fire codes are written in blood” - each warning sign came from experience). My results are quite good.  It’s as the saying goes, much like managing a team of junior devs.  It is easy to end up with a LOT of parallel implementors, reviewers, reworkers, and tons of CI, but it’s still so much vastly cheaper than humans that it doesn’t matter. Someone will make a LOT of money wringing out the inefficiencies from this workflow, because I think the “agent as replacement for third-world contracted junior dev” model is the one almost everyone is using right now.

> Say they cure cancer. A pet peeve of mine. People keep mouthing this same fantasy. But cancer is  so  many different cancers. And "the cure(s)" aren't just 1000 different drugs, but maybe 10,000 different candidates for each that pass into lab tests, of which maybe 1% make it to phase 1 trials, and of those maybe 10% make it all the way through phase 3, each after 5-10 years of clinical trials and $100s of millions invested each. For the most part, AI-related biotechs are largely focussing on accelerating the discovery of good candidates. But that's a tiny fraction of the pipeline, which includes lots of lab work (which  can  be automated) and clinical trials (which OTOH require actual human guinea pigs and years of observation and assessment). How do you meaningfully accelerate that? Presumably by improving the odds of success in phase 3 trials from your initial candidates. But nobody has proposed yet how LLMs can be a magic bullet here. At best they'll give you those 10,000 candidates per cancer type faster. But then you have all that lab work and clinical work to slog through, and all the likely failures you'll see in clinical trials. And there's just not enough data out there to train ML on to meaningfully improve the odds of success in clinical trials, since you'd really have to understand how your drugs work with all proteins and systems in every type of human body, e.g. "in silico" clinical trials. And we're only merely scratching the surface of that with stuff like OpenADMET. That is, we can't even model well "how a human body works", much less "how those mechanisms go wrong in each type of cancer". But even if you  could  do all that, for the cures you'd need to figure out what novel, unusual, out-of-distribution thing (relative to your human model) you can throw into the system to avoid the bad behavior, that doesn't kill the person or interfere with other systems or get degraded too quickly or ... tons of other stuff. Highly non-trivial. Maybe lower-hanging fruit is with a novel peptide or antibody, since those are better modeled with ML. But small drug-like molecules are galactic in number and not well modeled yet. ("Hey, what happens if I introduce this weird platinum-based drug into a body?"  Well yeah, cisplatin is used for chemotherapy, but the body of knowledge needed to assess platinum-based drugs in a human body just doesn't exist, and ML isn't gonna intuit it from known data, nor "learn it" since that would require going down to QM, and then integrating that into its model of all human peptides and pathways.) This is not a side-project for a chatbot company. Its a (multi-)generational project that requires buy-in from labs that can produce the requisite data. (And okay so maybe I'm fast-and-loose above. Ideally a single "cure" would be to fix the apoptosis pathway, i.e. repair the built-in cell-death path for fast reproducing cells. But cancer cells mutate quickly and evade known avenues. Perhaps there's a generic fix? Plausible but same reasoning applies: ML doesn't have enough data to intuit a solution, if one exists. And there's no reason, a prior, to assume that one does exist. Only hope.)

Not really, look at the definition of "STEALTH BOT" -- the only thing that nominally distinguishes it from a browser is the word "bot" which isn't itself defined, because the phrase "without prior disclosure of its identity and purpose" is something that a normal web browser doesn't do either. It can't even get it out of it via "a valid and accurate user-agent string", both because that clause says  or  and it still fails the second one, and because "a valid and accurate user-agent string" is a nonsense phrase. The Safari user agent strings start with "Mozilla" even though it's not. The Android ones do the same and then include "AppleWebKit" and "Mobile Safari" too. >  skill atrophy is real  It is also both a choice and avoidable. Atrophy happens when you trade understanding for productivity. Productivity benefits your employer and your KPIs, but not your understanding and your opportunities going forward. Understanding used to be an unavoidable of the exploration process, and writing documentation used to be the thing that never got done. As review of their understanding, and for the sake of my own cognitive debt, I would first ask them the question "How does it work?" and they usually couldn't answer. After a handful of tasks, they started preparing answers. This forth-and-back is still more shallow than getting the deep knowledge chiseled through hours of trial and error, debugging and wrong directions. Spending two hours to find a problem to realize you forgot to save or upload a file, or had an x instead of a y. I look back with nostalgia, and I wonder if there weren't always better ways, and we just get to pick them now. I can literally convert any task, solved or not, into a quiz that brings me towards understanding, in rainbow-colored pig latin.

> Nobody depends on AI for core operations. Financial failure of an AI lab wouldn’t make that AI disappear. If people depend on them (aka demand) the IP of the labs would be valuable, someone would purchase it in bankruptcy, and they would continue serving the model. There is basically no comparison to the credit market collapse, even though all of the simplified comparisons try to draw a straight line between the two. The real concern is different: The theory is that if the frontier labs start collapsing, they will argue that their failure is equivalent to the US losing AI supremacy, which is equivalent to losing the future if you believe AI is winner take all. The argument is that they’ll be financially reckless and then ask the government to backstop losses if it falters, both to retain their lead and to protect the overall economy. The other part that of this is the increasingly widespread belief that AI is a total bubble without demand and it’s all going to collapse because there’s no profits to be found at all because it’s all financial theater. That argument is harder to make if you’ve looked at the actual unit economics of these companies (hint: Anthropic isn’t subsidizing inference like so many believed). AI is not going away and the demand for compute will only increase. The question is how accurately these scale ups track it and if they’re going to dip below the insolvency threshold from getting it wrong. But if the companies blow up, the technology doesn’t go away. The model weights aren’t deleted. The ML engineers don’t retire. Companies get restructured, IP assets can be sold to new operators, and engineers move to new companies with new business models.

Ops is bifurcating in two: * AI-resistant organizations led by graybeards who refuse to send telemetry off-prem (to either observability vendors or to inference providers) and will be dragged, kicking and screaming, into the future, over their cold, dead bodies. There's a lot of large, conservative organizations in this category like banks and governments, where budgets are rubber-stamped and Don't Break It If It Ain't Broken attitudes are tacitly approved of. * AI-accepting organizations where Ops will go through the same great narrowing that Dev is going through now - build the dark factory and let it run. You do still need people who know what good architecture looks like and to shepherd changes to improve the overall system to make it more observable, scalable, and maintainable. You do still need Non-Functional Software Engineers who don't answer to Product, for the sheer political reason that you need people who have a long-term perspective, compared to Product that has a short-term perspective. The business will make decisions like "Vendor X is too expensive so we're migrating to Vendor Y" and you will need somebody to drive the agents to make that happen in a way that respects availability and compliance requirements. You probably don't need, in the long-term, a whole team of people to handle it, let alone a whole group or a whole division. At the end of the day... focus on being a strong engineer. Somebody will always be needed to take care of the trees.

I'm interested in this intersection of technical problems where we already have the tech to solve it, but the bottlenecks are social/legal/financial incentive. Recently there was an old lady in the family that had an appendicitis, an ambulance rejected her, and the next day it got worse, and at that point she was accepted, but it was a bit too late. One hypothesis is that triaging is hard and there's a lot of demand so things only go in when it's bad enough (considering there was medical insurance, they aren't charging per patient, so there's no incentive to take on more patients). But if that were the case, then preventive measures would actually reduce the total burden on their system. The more cynical hypothesis that I'm holidng is that that health system is maximizing for work, if there's 10 appendicitis per month, and they are all handled in time, that's maybe like 5 hours of billable hours per patient? But if the appendicitis becomes bad enough and there's a puncture, then you have infections, complications, the patients have to stay for weeks and often come back for checkups, we are looking at maybe 100 billable hours? So the financial incentive is there. In that sense what I want to add is that the title would be completely wrong, the solution is not for the hospital to pay 100$ for prevention, but for prevention to be more accurately priced, we should be paying 50k, and maybe even 100k for prevention, because we value it more than emergency action. In a broader economic sense, there's a lot of cases where there's a huge difference between the cost and the value, Shkreli got a lot of heat for surging up medicine prices, but I don't think it's immediately obvious that something should be valued in proportion to what it costs. Maybe if we price heart prevention at 100K, there would be more incentive for everyone involved to just get a fucking pill to those in need, imagine how many people would jump at that opportunity to make it happen, call centers, bureocrats, NOC support, legal teams, all dedicated to making sure a pill gets to the patient before a heart attack does.

I’m not a policy maker, but off the top of my head: For starters, I’d have Congress preemptively do what they would probably do post some AI disaster. Something like form a committee of academic researchers, security professionals, and other people who are incentivized to be skeptical and have them investigate the risks posed by the AI we have and what’s cooking. The aim would be take the risks seriously and propose policies that seek to mitigate those risks. I’d also, make more of an effort to cooperate with governments to establish some treaty-like agreements about how we will use AI in critical areas like warfare. We have these kind of agreements about biological and nuclear weapons. We can have them about AI weapons, too. Maybe this would cool down the arms race atmosphere. I would establish some kind of central-bank like authority whose members are protected from congressional and executive-branch meddling and whose mandate is to influence the development of AI in a way that’s universally agreed to be good society. Not sure how this would look and what their levers would be, but I think something similar to the Feds mandate to balance employment and inflation, but the AI version, would be worth exploring. Finally, I wouldn’t wait until AI has replaced people and hyper scalers are sitting on trillions to have a plan for how millions of people are supposed to make a living when they can’t find work anymore because agents and robots are doing the jobs they used to do. I think we’re still a ways away from that reality. But having a framework, better yet policies, in place would probably make people feel a lot better about the development of AI. If everyone knows they’re going to get a UBI check for 5K plus access to a solid state sponsored healthcare plan for them and their immediate family when AI makes us all redundant, I don’t think people would be so apprehensive to AI and data centers. Again, I’m not a policy maker. I’m sure there are a bunch of externalities that people can point out to poke holes in my ideas. Be my guest. Sitting around doing what amounts to jack shit while the technology that powers the internet seems increasingly vulnerable to the technology we’re building and distributing as fast as possible definitely is not the way to go. I'll take a crack at this one. I've been using matrix and element for over a decade as my main messenger, and it's great, but it also does suck. I even use it for my business chat. It's pretty much the most popular federated encrypted client right now, and it seems to have taken over XMPP's lead. So here's a nice list/rant about why matrix/element sucks. 1. I spent 15 minutes last month helping my business partner sign onto ElementX on his second phone. He's signed on his PC and his primary phone, but the second phone was very difficult. Basically type username and password, but now you have to verify with emoji. How do you do that? Well, sometimes it pops up on your other clients that a new client needs verification. Sometimes the popup never shows, and there's no way to find it. But we found it eventually. Verify via emoji. Great! Let's do it. Oops, it timed out before he could finish. Apparently it has a super short timer that even I struggle with it. Eventually we gave up and used the recovery key, which worked, but you know many people are going to lose that key since it's not a password they can just memorize. Most other messengers, it's just username, password, and then click the email confirmation link. Boom, easy. 2. Audio/Video calling/conferencing. There are apparently 3(?) different technologies in Element alone, depending on which version of Element (desktop, web, mobile). The "old" one is jitsi. The new p2p one appears to be only available to clients that aren't Element? Or you can only create conference rooms in those other clients (commet?), but you can join them from any client. But then those new rooms are sometimes not join-able from Element clients. They just don't appear in the room list at all. Even clicking a link to the room says it's the wrong "room version", but it's a freshly-created room. So I delete the room and make another new one. But now it's a Jitsi room and it doesn't work in this other Element client (all first-party actual Element clients, and all broken in slightly different ways!). So... it's working now, but only after lots of trial and error and lots of cussing from my business partner. And I have to somehow justify that this is better than using Slack/Discord/whatever corporate thing. 3. The official client is fragmented. On mobile, there is Element (classic) and ElementX. You're _supposed_ to use ElementX, since it's the new one, but ElementX does not have all the features of Element (classic), so you might need the Element (classic) client for those things. But Element (classic) is not getting updated, so you're left in the cold as far as updates and the new features (meaning you might not even be able to cross-verify your clients, or join video calls, spaces, etc.) 4. The official matrix server (synapse) is pretty slow. I hosted a couple small communities (~100 people or so?), and synapse somehow kept getting overloaded and crashing. Maybe it needed more than 4GiB, but that seems kind of silly. There are decent 3rd-party clients (continuwuity is my current favorite), but there's no migration path from one server to another without wiping your entire database and starting fresh. So.... my main homeserver is kind of stuck on synapse. 5. Bridges. Yes, you can bridge anything to anything, but have you actually tried it? Interface is super clunky. You have to run a separate bridge service, make sure it swaps keys with the matrix server via a yaml configuration dance, then talk to the bridge's bot in a dedicated matrix channel with special commands that may or may not get your bridge working. I've used signal, discord, telegram, and irc bridges, and they're all a mess in one way or another. My most recent attempt was with the signal bridge. I made the mistake of enabling end-to-end encryption. One day, the bridge server restarted and lost all its encryption keys. Cool, now all the bridged rooms are dead. So naturally, I delete the bridge service and re-configure it from scratch. Now it doesn't work because its bridge bot username was already taken by the previous instance with the lost encryption keys. And I can't just delete that bridge bot user because _matrix does not allow deleting users ever!_. So now I have broken signal bridge rooms and broken signal bot users that I can't ever delete, even with the admin panel. So naturally I open up a postgresql client and delete them manually. Oops, now my matrix database is broken in ways I cannot even begin to comprehend. Because deleting users is not allowed. So now I just can't have a signal bridge. _maybe_ there's a way to make it work, but I've been programming and sys-admin'ing for over 20 years, and it's just beyond me. I'm going to have to (again!) wipe out my homeserver and start over, losing all my messages and contacts (again!). XMPP had very nice transport services, and Psi+ had a very nice UI for configuring and organizing them. 6. Multi-identity support is lacking in all the official and most community clients. If I have a work account and a personal account, I need to start two separate Element clients. Each one is a hefty electron app, and they all have the same systray icon, so I need to trial+error every time to open the right one to message someone. So far, there's only one client I tried that had proper multi-account, and I think it was commet. It was ok, but I hated that it was a flutter desktop app where every click felt super unresponsive. So I went back to Element. Most XMPP clients have multi-identity built-in. I'm not going to use my work identity for personal chat, just like I'm not going to use my hackernews account to message co-workers. 7. No message auto-deletion. Many people like to claim that Element is more secure than Signal. It is not. If you live in an oppressive country where things you say can easily result in prison or torture, you need more than E2E encryption. You need messages to be gone. You can't trust that your device or your friend's device won't get confiscated and forced to reveal your password. Even the United States has forced device unlocking at the borders. Signal (and Confide, and even Telegram) have automatically deleting messages, so even with the keys, there's nothing to see. Matrix stores messages forever. Aside from some complicated server-side setting, there's no way to automatically delete them. You have to right-click and manually delete EVERY message if you want future privacy. Nobody's going to do that. And I tried enabling the synapse settings for auto-deleting messages, but they didn't work. It seems that feature isn't really tested, or it's documented poorly. 8. The spam/CSAM problem when running a public community. The admin tools are a bit lacking, so without some considerable expertise, it's often not worth even having a community matrix server. So folks just make a discord instead, which has actual moderation tools builtin. Yes, I know there are external moderation tools you can install, but why should that be required? 9. The protocol is too complex to make full-featured 3rd-party clients. This isn't IRC where you can make a basic client in 3 lines of perl. You'll notice that the 3rd-party clients are all lacking in some features of Element, the official client. Even the official ElementX client lacks features of Element Classic. Most folks are stuck on the official electron-based Element client, which has a fairly clunky UX (try explaining to your grandma how to cross-verify clients). This list is just off the top of my head. I could probably write a whole book on the problems with the matrix ecosystem. But again, matrix is the best we have. IRCv3 hasn't really caught on, and the need for an IRC bouncer to receive offline messages isn't commonly excepted in 2026. XMPP was/is ok, but it hasn't been commonly used since Google Hangouts pulled the bait+switch on us 10+. I keep thinking I should really just go back to XMPP, or start using delta.chat since "everyone" has an email address. I often can't even get fairly technical folks (who write code by hand, etc) to use Element, even if I do all the server setup and just hand them the keys. It's too hard for most folk. It's too hard for me, and I've been maintaining my own matrix servers for 7+ years. I maintain 3 matrix servers right now. One synapse, and two continuwuity. NixOS makes it pretty easy to maintain servers, actually, as long as they're not open to the public. And if anyone asks me "what should we use instead?", I'd probably say XMPP or IRC. And we know neither of those is perfect, either, and nothing open source and federated is as easy to onboard like Discord, Signal, or Slack. But even though Element/Matrix sucks, it still works well enough for me to use it as my main communication. At least until I finish my own multi-protocol messenger. Which I started about 6 years ago and haven't had time to work on. Disclosure: I wrote some of the code on Confide's backend back in 2021. I do not currently work at that company and am not promoting or un-promoting the app in any way.

pyon is basically correct. --- technical details --- CLRS (3rd edition) defines three types of amortized cost analysis. The first type ("aggregate analysis") requires us to show that for all sequences of  n  operations, the total actual cost of performing those operations in that sequence is less than some function  T(n) . We can then say that the amortized cost of all such operations is  T(n) / n . This makes it necessary that cheap operations precede expensive ones. The second type ("the accounting method") is different: we assign potentially-inaccurate prices to all operations. These prices will be constant regardless of the actual cost of performing those operations. Conceptually, an operation is in "credit" if its actual cost is less than its assigned price, and it is in a state of owing if its actual cost is more than its assigned price. We must then assign prices that make it possible to show that, for all sequences of operations, the total actual cost of all operations from the start of the sequence to point  n  within it is less than the total amortized price assigned by our price schedule. (Stated another way, while an individual operation is free to "owe", a sequence of operations may never be in an "owing" state.) If we can prove that, we are justified in making a claim about the amortized cost of the operations we considered. (Under this method, the amortized cost of an operation is equal to the price we assigned it.) This also makes it necessary that cheap operations precede expensive ones. The third type ("the potential method") defines a potential function which evaluates the state of the data structures maintained by the algorithm. ("Potential" in the sense of potential energy, which can be stored and later released.) It then says that the amortized cost of an operation is equal to the actual cost, plus the difference in "potential state" caused by the operation. Conceptually, if potential is raised, the amortized cost was higher than the actual cost (and has built up a buffer that later operations may draw down), and if it is lowered, the amortized cost was lower than the actual cost. As before, we must show that no sequence of operations can place the data structure into a state of negative potential. Cheap operations must precede expensive ones. ------ Now, why was pyon telling you you should be ashamed of your post? It's almost certainly these two paragraphs: >> If you read more about big-O, you may see the word “amortized” thrown around. That’s a fancy word for “average,” meaning that individual occurrences don’t all behave exactly the same, but over the long run, averaging over many operations, the behavior has a certain characteristic. >> The analysis we’ve been doing is for the average behavior. Lots of operations can behave much worse in unusual circumstances. Adding a key in a dict and looking up a key are O(1), which is true for typical data. But if you understand the internals of dicts, you can carefully craft a set of keys that will perform terribly, with O(N) behavior. Filling that dict would take O(N²) time. Your post has confused average-case analysis with amortized analysis. (And it makes this problem worse by implying that the two terms refer to the same concept.) The  point  of amortized analysis is that you cannot see worse performance than the amortized cost. An amortized analysis is deterministic and averages runtime costs over the different operations that are present in a sequence of operations beginning from a given initial state; an average-case analysis is stochastic and averages runtime costs of a single operation over many different performances of that operation against different initial states. These two terms are not synonymous and they don't belong to the same universe of terminology; if we're thinking about "average-case analysis", then an amortized analysis is a type of "worst-case analysis", not a type of average-case analysis. The first paragraph I quoted tells us that you're talking about amortized analysis, but you aren't: the example you provide is of an average-case analysis. If the amortized cost of adding a key to a dictionary were O(1), it would be impossible for adding a sequence of N keys to that dictionary to take more than O(N) time. (As is in fact the case for the Python list.append example you mention beforehand.)

Everything I am suggesting here is what an internal team with full ownership of the network should do. An external team could chisel little by little, and progress the network in phases. What is shared here is a general direction. I am sure some people I know where all they do is networking could tell me harshly some of these ways could be done better, and often these people are right ; but sometimes these same people are actually wrong and don't fully consider the positions of people in IT roles at companies that aren't ISPs. All suggested below is not necessarily the ultimate way but a general direction. _ >> can only get IPv4 addresses through the ISP DHCP ISP-owned IP addresses, either of legacy IP or IPv6, are capricious and can suddenly change, as you experienced recently. I suggest to adopt a mindset of "our network" and "their network", rather than functionally have your network be a passive extension of their network by using their IP addresses. The router announcements (IPv6 RA) or DHCP (IPv4) for any IP addresses within your network should always be issued by devices controlled solely by our organization. NAT64 and tunnels exist, any upstream ISP is not a blocker. Modern Linux has eBPF and eXpress Data Path. Both Linux and FreeBSD (use HardenedBSD if you can) have DPDK. They can make for surprisingly high performance edge routers on x86_64 server boxes over a decade old, exceeding what most campuses or even datacenter footprints actually need and at low cost. Even without eBPF & XDP or DPDK, these on x86_64 are often "good enough" for router and firewall. DNS running on these or adjacent boxes internal to the organization is essential. The addresses at the gateways, either of IPv4 or IPv6, can be made highly available with VRRPv3. IPv6 has an elegant way to handle multiple upstream ISPs without VRRP or CARP at the gateways, but even Linux is just recently implementing what may only be a piece of them (the BSDs will later), some mention of them here  https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50143420  _ What I would do, which is opinionated so I'm not necessarily suggesting others do it, assuming tunneling will be involved: if the organizational wherewithal is there to register an AS and do BGP, is pay the AUD 500 fee to register an AS and have a chunk of IPv6 space for to use IPv6 GUA addresses that officially belong to the organization. If not, which is often enough the case because we know how some organizations can be slow (not making any assumptions about your's), the remaining avenue is to use IPv6 ULA addresses which are the spiritual counterpart to IPv4 RFC1918 addresses. You can embed MAC addresses in IPv6 ULA addresses, like the MAC 82c6.7943.acb2 put in an IPv6 like     fc00:5007:6525:2001:3003:82c6:7943:acb2
  
and use DHCPv6 to always assign a specific IPv6 ULA address to a specific MAC address, where you have thought through the potential information-disclosure implications and you are certain you want to do that. Then I would use IPv4-only ISP paths for what they're good for: dumb paths to tunnel IPv6 packets to where there is proper internet. For the option with an AS, BGP announcements on the other side of the tunnel. Personally I would do SCION on the gateways and out the other side of the tunnel, but you don't want to do SCION unless you are also crazy (like a fox). For the IPv6 ULA option, PAT which is the spiritual counterpart to IPv4's NAT but is also technologically simpler. With IPv6 ULA and no tunneling, NAT64 and DNS64 can work for outbound. Site to site tunnels will be tricky no matter what. Tailscale, ZeroTier, Netbird, and similar may be able to do much of the work for you ; these should run in a DMZ on another side of a router/firewall that filters the appropriate IPv6 ULA prefixes. I would try to see if I could make vanilla Wireguard work with NAT traversal techniques using some cloud-hosted VMs that help with the "hole punching", but not everyone would do that. There aren't many options that will all work well but almost always more than one option that can work well, all subject to the specific site and inter-organizational resources. _ >> dropping IPv4 support might mean dropping support for older devices For as long as it makes organizational sense to continue using these devices, put them behind an OpenBSD box that performs NAT46 and DNS46, with IPv4 addresses statically mapped to IPv6 addresses, maybe ones that contain the MAC addresses of the devices. With Salt or Ansible, such a scheme with NAT, DNS, DHCP configuration may all be templatized and in perfect alignment, and is scalable. Authoritative inventory of canonical identifiers/names versioned with Git, what Ansible calls "inventory", is imperative. Sometimes this looks like a couple of old x86_64 boxes doing CARP (similar to VRRP) on the IPv4 side for a few dozen or couple hundred devices downstream. Sometimes this looks like, in a handful of distant corners of the larger network, a cheap single-board computer between a single device and the rest of the network ; without a wifi chip or the wifi chip removed by heating (board-repair style), unless downstream of a wifi AP. _ >> the ISP which is THE biggest ISP in Argentina, they don't offer IPv6
>> The ISP brand is Personal, local corp is Telecom Argentina S.A, Asynchronous System Number AS7303, trades as TEO in NYSE I think, owned by Grupo Clarin which comes is a traditional Media and news company. I can think of some service provider network engineers that would gladly drop all of Argentina's IPv4 off the entire internet and "IPv6 prefix announcements welcome", if the business sides would let them do it. Something like this will probably start happening sooner than people think.

I've been doing multi-agent development for a while now and I've been very happy with the outcome. I disagree with the approach of creating a fleet of "persona" agents and just letting them rip. Instead, I use a standard SDLC pipeline with stages that produce artifacts and gates that evaluate them. The gates have both deterministic and stochastic (LLM as a judge) components. The blend depends on the artifact: prose leans heavily on LLMs, where code has a lot of tests. I work by having a discussion with claude code about what I'm trying to do and how it might be built. I ask it how its proposal fits into the existing bounded contexts and if it is reusing the existing patterns and libraries. Once it can give me an approach I like, I have it create a plan. This uses a skill and it has guidance on the structure and contents of the plan. It is mostly prose, so the deterministic checks just look for the sections in the correct order. The LLM reviewer is a different model entirely to avoid bias and it is agentic, so it can (and does) explore the code and is prompted to verify the plan is correct both in the abstract and in the context of the code. Once approved, it moves to breaking the plan into one or "releases" which are batches of tasks. Another gate, then to coding, which is where it fans out to multiple implementing agents. Another gate. As I said, very standard SDLC. I get asked this question a lot, so I wrote it up with a guide on how to do it on the second to last page.  https://michael.roth.rocks/research/543-hours

> Good developers’ caution about agentic development comes from knowing that built isn’t the same as working in production...I always felt there was something else, another fear hiding behind those obvious ones. It's not fear.  It's experience.  I've seen the kind of code agents write.  And it's too often crap even when it "works".  This isn't about beautiful code.  It's about what we've built actually making sense to a, hopefully talented, software engineer. Maybe more important than that, it's about taking the time to build the mental models that facilitate product development and the next iterations of coding.  When agents write all the software, the majority of engineers I've seen, including myself, lose almost all context to what is actually going on at anything but a very high almost laughable level.  And they then become almost completely dependent on the agent for the next iteration of development b/c they don't really understand what is there currently. Does this matter?  From a software perspective, it depends on what you are building and for whom. From a human perspective, it depends on the human.  I've seen good developers that I trust historically churn out crap code with agents because it was just too much to review.  And there is some kind of weird addiction like thing happening in our brains when using AI that makes it incredibly difficult for us to slow down and review all the code it writes.  In part b/c agents are great at crapping out 3K line PRs like it's nobody's business.  But it needs to be someone's business to understand what we are shipping for anything but non-trivial projects.  And truly understanding 3K line PRs hour after hour is just not sustainable for most of us.  Our eyes glaze over and we just ship it because that's what we do now as an industry. I think wary is the wrong term.  I've learned agentic development's strengths and weaknesses.  And the tools, as they work currently, churn out code at a rocket's pace that any good software engineer would immediately reject in years past.  I don't like their code, I don't like how their code development process interacts with my brain.  It's not waryness, it's dislike and mistrust. So, yes, they can be assistants.  And they can even write code.  But I think in much smaller chunks than most people are using them these days. The idea that we should build software factories and/or otherwise just turn agents loose and isolate humans to the product/QA level is insane to me.  But I understand why we are here and I realize that a large portion of the business and dev community likes this new model. I'm hoping that not doing it that way will end up be a competitive advantage in the long run.  Both for the software we are producing and for the devs that are creating it.

I attribute much of Stack Overflow's decline to a mismatch of scaling... and that mismatch is in part what lead to the perceived hostility by askers and answerers.  Overcorrection and changes (frequently removing of curation tools) often made this worse.  (Part of this is inspired by a recent post on meta.stackexchange about how corporate is redoing question deleting and Shog's answer to it  https://meta.stackexchange.com/a/420032  ) The scaling focuses around discoverability, (the rate of) asking questions, and the amount of time available for people to curate (which includes helping new users get onboarded). Much of the early days of Stack Overflow, discoverability was trivial.  It was easy to find an interesting question because few things were asked and this was the days when there was a  lot  of changes.  We're dealing with 2008 and beyond - there were a lot of new frameworks and languages being updated then... Spring 3, Backbone, Knockout, Angular, React, Vue, Spring Boot 1, Java 7 and eventually Java 8. This was a time of rapid change and the experts were answering on Stack Overflow - and it was scaling up to meet that demand with additional tools. But it also started becoming a place where students were posting questions (every September you'd get the "how do you draw a triangle with stars?" questions 20 times a day in the Java or Python tags...) This started being visible in 2010 with question quality and by 2014 it was a full on epidemic. One part of this is that the original community of people who followed Jeff and Joel's blogs and helped barn raise the site had gotten smaller as an overall portion of the site because of that explosive growth.  Some people wanted it to be a place where any user could get help with a question (and closing questions was antithetical to that) and others were looking for it to be more of a wikipedia.  That conflict still simmers. Another part of this is that a smaller and smaller percent of the overall user base was using the curation tools available.  Fewer people were closing questions (that really did need to be closed) and helping onboard new users with expectations.  When there are 6000 new questions a day that represents a  lot  of work for the volunteers to try to onboard them.  Initially, everyone came from the same point and there wasn't much onboarding needed.  With its growth, a lot of new people were coming to it from the approach that it was a forum or immediate feedback chat. That growth without scaling up the tools for onboarding and curation (making it  easier  to do) meant that the people trying to help new users and make discovery of well written questions easier had less time per user (or question) to do so... and got increasingly curt - they couldn't spend 5 minutes per question anymore and instead were trying to do things in 30 seconds or less. This was the beginning of "Stack Overflow is unfriendly." The attempt that corporate had from this, instead of making it easier to help people took away curation tools and close reasons were made more specific... which in turn meant that the people trying to close questions to make discoverability of well written questions on the home page easier were incredibly pedantic in order to meet those reasons. Some of the tooling is set up to be able to handle 6000 questions per day, and scales poorly back to having 100 questions per day. The user base of Stack Overflow at 2 months old is  very  different than Stack Overflow today, even if it has the same question rate.  There are very few people who are around to help onboard users (diamond mods if you read this - there's 25 of you and 100 questions per day... you can spend 5 minutes per new question per day to help onboard the user for expectations and still have half an hour a day for other moderation tasks). Many of the people who did curation when SO was growing and at its peak have become disappointed with Stack Overflow and while they may look at it to see if its a site where their contributions would again be appreciated... though the changes that corporate appears to want have been additional curtailment of curation tools and have even proposed removing close votes all together (  https://meta.stackoverflow.com/questions/438185/the-company-...  ). --- Stack Overflow is mostly dead.  It lingers on, but every change that is being attempted or proposed in trying to get more "engagement" takes it further and further from being a place where new knowledge is collected and collated. I would attribute this mostly to there aren't any curators left - so everything they try building turns into a mess.  Corporate has leaned too hard on the community to do curation and diamond mods have largely stopped doing curation in favor of moderation. With low activity and the largest ratio of staff and diamond mods to active users, this would be an excellent time for those two groups to completely take up the task of curation and onboarding to set a new standard for how it should be done... and if they aren't willing to do it, that really suggests that the final nail in the coffin is in place waiting to get hammered.

Hey HN, I'm Colin. I built Parley so that multiple coding-agents using different models or harnesses can collaborate over a live IRC channel, with me in the chat using any IRC client. Each session can deliver messages to the channel using the `parley send` CLI tool call and sessions receive messages using their harnesses' channel or queue interface. All messages received on the channel are marked as coming from a peer so a session can never take another agent's message as coming from me. It works on Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode. Parley is a standalone Go CLI, stdlib only, Apache 2.0. It runs its own ergo IRC server on 127.0.0.1 (loopback only), so nothing touches a public network. I built it with Claude Code and Codex. The motivation came from wanting to explore a more interactive collaboration structure between agents rather than a simple sub-agent delegation model. It allows running multiple long-running agents with assigned roles which I provide as their first message in the chat. My typical setup so far assigns a builder role to execute build and review tasks, a planner role to supervise the overall goal, task ordering, and scheduling and an ops role to handle everything related to infrastructure, operations, deployments, secops, etc. All 3 can now interactively update/sync each other at every turn and start collaborating across their roles. There is a configurable breaker to pause the session until I post if there are too many messages in a short window. I use it on macOS; on Linux the test suite passes in CI but I haven't run it live.  https://github.com/colinsurprenant/parley#what-a-line-looks-...

hey Nishit, kevan here. sorry we completely missed your comment and your question short answer is no, the policy engine doesn't know where an argument came from across calls. each call is judged on its own: which agent, which end user it's acting for (plus the delegation chain), which grant, which operation and the params on the request. so in your example the contractor's send passes if their policy allows it we put the controls at the two ends instead of following the data through the middle
- write side: the CEO's grant posting into a shared channel is its own call, so you can require approval for it or just deny it
- send side: we parse sends into recipients, so a contractor can be limited to emailing inside the company domain, or anything external needs a human approval on the exact frozen request every call is audited with the agent, end user and grant, and calls in the same run share a trace id. your case spans two sessions though, so the thing linking them is the slack message itself, not a trace your noise point is honestly why we haven't done taint tracking yet, the "user typed the address but it was also in tool output" case is exactly the hard bit. it's a really interesting scenario though, we'll look into whether it makes sense for us to support this kind of thing natively.

Unfortunately, laws and regulations aren't exactly  clear  and over time situations change so one important role of the court system is interpreting how, when and whether the words in a law apply in a specific context. Courts at different levels do this all the time as cases with unique situations arise. Sometimes it's as simple as deciding if a horse counts as a vehicle in a state law which says "no vehicles on this type of road." Assuming that ruling survives appeals without being overturned, the judge will have justified the basis and, hopefully, some clear reasoning for  why  a horse does or doesn't count as a vehicle. That judge's ruling then becomes part of the "precedent" (aka 'body of case law') attached to that law. In effect, such precedents  become  part of the law since they can clarify if and how the law applies in certain situations. So whether some action is or isn't against a law can't solely be determined by just reading the law. You have to do some interpretation, which includes looking up any relevant precedents and weighing them. A single prior ruling from one local municipal court has low weight. The main job of the Supreme Court is resolving conflicting precedents set by lower courts, so a SCOTUS ruling has a lot of weight and multiple SCOTUS rulings over time, each successively refining and narrowing (or occasionally reversing) their prior interpretations, carries maximum weight. All of this happens in the open and, in the long run, I think SCOTUS manages to eventually get most things, if not perfect, pretty close to right. Hence, the answer to "Is this legal" can be a bit tricky when the law is new or there aren't decades of court precedents. So lawyers have to do research and assess how a court would  probably  rule on a given situation. That's called "a formal legal opinion" and it's provided in writing, usually including research and justifications, like references to existing case law, as well as legal reasoning supporting the opinion. Anyone can hire a lawyer to research and assess if X action violates Y law (but if you get sued for relying on the lawyer's opinion, they won't be on the hook - you will). It's called an opinion because that's really all it is. A simple observation here is that historically inter people communication is the main scaling bottleneck in software teams. It's what's behind the main premise in the mythical man month that adding more people to a team makes it slower. You increase the man months, but you are adding so much overhead that it's a net loss. It's why big software companies struggle getting big things done whereas small and nimble startups tend to run circles around those. Google, Apple, Amazon, and Microsoft are great examples of companies that are really struggling with doing anything outside of the stuff they are already know how to do despite adding people by the thousands/tens of thousands. The more people they have the less likely any of them is going to be to do something completely new and different. How does AI impact all this? It makes the problem (inter people communication) much worse. Imagine five people doing things manually. They have to sync up regularly. But there's only so much they can do in a day so they can stay in sync relatively easy. Scale that to 50. Now your meeting overhead becomes very non trivial. Now add AI to the mix. Each of these people goes off and maxes out their tokens every day. They are refactoring, adding new sub systems/products, new UIs, etc. How do they coordinate their actions? How are they going to communicate their intentions and actions to each other. How do they brief each other on what's already been done? The day to day scope of the massive amount of changes done by each of those individuals quickly grows way beyond whatever fits in typical/reasonable meeting structures. So, all the obvious things start happening: people either don't communicate or communicate poorly. They work against each other, break each other's work, etc. Everybody has a hard time staying on whatever is happening. The easy implication is exactly what we see happening in most big organizations: not much happening at all. They were already bottle necked on their size. AI made the problem much worse and as a result they aren't getting more done. At best they are maybe getting about the same stuff done with a bit less people. AI clearly favors setups where you can minimize all of the communication. Small 1-3 person teams are probably a lot more optimal here. They always were and e.g. Jeff Bezos figured that out early in the life of Amazon (the two pizza rule). But AI just makes it much more obvious. Remove the need to sync lots of people and you free up time to actually do stuff (with or without AI). The same dynamic probably holds to some extent with using multiple agents. If you are burning a lot of tokens and time on getting agents to sync with each other, that overhead is only going to get worse if you add more agents probably. And if you need to be in the loop to micro manage them, you become the bottleneck. Even if you just work by yourself. The trick is providing enough autonomy so you don't have to micro manage as much. And structuring your agents to minimize the amount of other agents each agent has to sync up with. The two pizza rule still holds.

Math is an interesting case. Arguably a lot of the groundwork was already there. There’s a huge body of academic literature that’s historically been difficult for humans to draw on for various reasons. It’s relatively easier for LLMs to mine all of that for relevant prior work that it can recycle into proof segments to try. And we have theorem proving software that it can use to try out these proof segments and validate them. That creates a tight, self-contained, and relatively inexpensive feedback loop that lends itself well to a host of agents grinding away, as long as you have budget to pay for all that LLM inference. I’m not sure the same conditions exist in other fields that deal with real world phenomena. Experiments to test hypotheses about biology or physics can take years and cost millions of dollars to run. They rarely scale down to the millipennies and milliseconds scale that makes letting a swarm of agents throw a bunch of shit at the wall and see what sticks a feasible option for finding mathematical proofs.

And the amazing thing is, everything has just a single representation: window positions displayed as text automatically have 2 way bindings across widgets, because they are the same data. But even with agents doing everything, 2 things creep up. First is in JS/TS, all these binding problems are solved 1000x already. You can fake shared memory with callbacks and the agent won't lose track. In GT you move the cursor around, and have to decide at what point do you convert a widget representation to source representation, and when to restore the widget: is it a delay? is it after changing lines? is it after you move off the text? before or after the whitespace? There's a package for that somewhere in npm that answered all these questions, and it has tables, and it's performant. It doesn't do the 2% stuff that GT does using its magical shared memory representation (which also makes TS->smalltalk porting not straightforward), but you can still tape over it with sheer optimized code. The second thing is that GT got really slow with all the data structure re-interpreting and rerendering. As "dirty" as bb is in reloading dynamic code, the runtimes are so optimized, I wanted the markdown nodes to be GPU-accelerated in bb, and it turns out they already were.

Thanks for your interest. I (very respectfully!) disagree that most, or indeed that any, of my decisions aren't worth recording. I have an explicit "completist" attitude to epistemic materials (records). First, we have LOTS of space now and decision records are cheap: We now can get several terabytes for a hundred or a couple hundred dollars. Storing the record of decisions is a drop in the bucket. In practical terms, taking the time to specify project-specific records helps ensure adherence and faithfulness from models; but very often, I've found the cross-projects benefits are also extraordinary (more on that in the third point!). Second, as I mentioned in some other comments, the methodology instructs models to surface all uncertainties and all doubts (Secondary Directive) and to commit all discussions (Prime Directive), but to surface these as ORRCF-formatted questions, with ORRCF (pronounced ORR-ssef) = Options, Recommendation, Rationale, Confidence, Falsifier. It's a way of surfacing doubts where your cognitive load is reduced, because everything you need to think about is brought up in the same screen, and you get to either endorse to recommendation knowingly, or override it with exactly what needs to be captured in disagreement. Third, when I disagree with the model's recommendation (or even when I agree, but have extended requirements, caveats, ideas, etc.) everyone of my decisions is fully thought-out: When I make decisions of deployment platforms based on predicted economics factors, or when I decide not to use Meta-created or Meta-related libraries for ethical reasons, or when I make decisions about modal grouping in user interfaces, or principles under which the user must be guaranteed never to have drafts clobbered, those are all worth capturing. All of these decisions compound, in the sense that, with the right indexing they can be referred to in the future: I can point to a set of records rather than specify, or I can have the model send a sub-agent to send a cluster of past projects for relevant decision records. At least, for me (perhaps because of my neurotype), it is more enjoyable and efficient to think deliberately slowly about each decision, to fully specify my thinking factoring everything I know — and to do so, knowing that now it will pay off in the sense that I will never have to explain myself again because I've put down my best thinking on this problem and can cite it forever in my future projects. I am decoupling thinking and doing, and it's really compounding over time, and producing sustainable epistemic scaffolding to my projects. To be very concrete, here's the loop of work in this model:
- You do an audio braindump of your thoughts
- Models iterate with you until it is well-defined enough that they can put together an initial draft of one or more ADRs (possibly 10-20 if you are bootstrapping a project)
- Any more-granular tensions are now surfaced to you as ORRCF-formatted QST questions, and you get to look at them in whatever order you want (including in orders suggested by models through the QuestionTour feature)
- You look at the questions and most of the times approve the recommendation, but occasionally, there's an opportunity for you to inject a zest of what makes you, Selkirk, your special epistemic patina, and you override the recommendation with something new, bold, beautiful, unique the models couldn't have foreseen even with what they are starting to know, through the previous records, about you
- After answering, the models, build, build, build, build, build, autonomously, and only surface for air if there are new tensions that surface
- Meanwhile as you see the results take shape, you are hungry for more and start brain dumping more ideas, which they structure, surface questions, which you answer, they build, iterate, and so on
- The records are what the models understand and what they need you for, it's not a post-hoc ceremony, it speeds up the process! I hope this makes sense?

Hi HN. I run a one-person company in Taiwan. MindThread is a Threads scheduler with paying users here, and it already had a REST API. This release wraps it for agents: a CLI (`npx mindthread-cli`) and an MCP server (`npx -y mindthread-mcp`, or hosted at  https://mindthread.tw/api/mcp , registry id io.github.ppcvote/mindthread). Your agent can draft posts in the account's voice, publish or schedule text, images, carousels and video, work a queue, read insights, and review reply drafts from "cloud patrol", which searches Threads for your keywords. Everything in this release goes through Meta's official Threads API, so no passwords. (A separate, Taiwan-only browser extension exists and is not part of this.) The part I care about most is control. Each key has allow, ask or deny per permission (publish now, schedule, send replies, turn on patrol). With ask, the call returns `approval_required` and a link, and nothing goes out until the owner confirms on mindthread.tw. In the CLI that is exit code 3, so the agent stops instead of retrying. Defaults for a new live key: publish now, sending replies, enabling patrol and loosening guardrails ask first; scheduling a post 30+ minutes ahead is allowed, and you can set it to ask. Content rules (length, banned phrases, only numbers from your fact list) are checked by the server on every API write and again at publish time. With `enforce: block` a violating post is refused; the default is `warn`, which only flags it. Limits: Threads only. Free plan is 1 account, 3 posts a day and 50 calls a day per live key, and Meta's per-profile caps apply on top. The MCP server lacks the thread, webhook and A/B tools the CLI has. The CLI and bridge are MIT; the service is hosted. No signup needed to look around: `curl  https://mindthread.tw/api/mcp ` lists the tools, and `tools/list`, `get_playbook` and `list_formulas` work without a key. A free account gives you a `mt_test_` sandbox key. A `mt_test_` key simulates every write. Feedback I want: is per-permission ask the right granularity, and what would you need before letting an agent post for you?

For each, I will look at datasheets, reviews, manuals, search for common issues, availability of spare parts, etc. Dozens of tabs per product, but I will close most of these, and leave the most salient ones open. Prune the whole product from the tree if I can eliminate it. And so on (availability at retailers, second hand stores, etc), until the task is done. Obviously the depth will vary from one task to another, but this is how I usually work on any topic, including literature review. So I only have "root nodes" with the next 20-ish tabs related to it.
