>Debugging can be done by writing/deleting/modifying code (e.g., write a test and run it, or add log statements, or remove a line and re-run the program, etc.), or by running shell tools We can end with things like "drinking cofee is an essential part of debugging for me". Debugging is an integration work, just like architecture planning, so it's somehow tied to plain english skills, reading docs, running whatever existing commands there are, parsing tools output is very important thing. Another point on which we should reach an agreement is the definition of debugging, as I suspect you may have your own definition. Fixing compiler error is not debugging. Glancing over source code is not debugging. Debugging is characterized by running a program and comparing the actual outcome with the expected one — implying finding the exact part of the source code responsible for the problem. Meatbags often do not read the full related code, and sometimes are not even experts in that particular programming language, or simply don't own the code and have hard time digging into it. Countrary, LLM-s excel at bruteforce code sifting and spitting two more 200-lines python scripts each minute. Still, even with AI debugging is not just "read and write code" — it's rather a high level skill with code read-writing being the largest hammer in the belt. Hammer so large AI will write several large scripts rather than use existing simple command. >It's also fun to write your own debugging tools by the way - just imagine any debugging workflow you think is good, write the tool, give the agent some tips how to use it, and they'll do great. It's so good, you should really try it. You conflate crutches with features. LLM-s absolutely suck at interactive tools, so they have to compensate with their strongest side: writing-reading code. Not because that's the absolutely most efficient way to debug, but because the economy is shaped differently in the world of AI. Running application manually, manually collecting logs, and then feeding them into AI is not "debugging made by AI" — it's the debugging made by human while AI doing the "code sifting" part of the debugging process. >> The fact that you personally do both things does not mean everybody and everything does it this way. >I don't, but LLMs certainly do. When I look at my agent doing 1000 characters one-line python script for testing/debugging, I do realize there is no way it could be a common code-writing skill, regular python code does not look like this, the skill requires some special understanding of agentic loops, it cannot be from pre-training dataset. And you definitely cannot say that "being able to write code" automatically enabled "being able to debug" — just try any pre-2025 model that is decent at code writing but not trained for modern tools/harness (I'm pretty sure some newer models also lack this ability, but such models are harder to spot). I'm pretty sure everybody here tested pre-2025 models, it's really nothing to argue about. >Programming and debugging is self-evidently part of the same training loop. Agents write code, validate it and adjust trajectory. I would suggest you to re-examine some fundamental explanation of how LLM training actually happens, because it seems to me you don't differentiate pre-training and post-training stages (and post-training has lots of flavors in it). Trying to train LLM for agentic coding and debugging before it learns basic code patterns is a huge waste of resources. "Never say never" — if you manage to generate dozens of billions of agentic training sets, you can probably end up doing "coding+debugging pre-training", but so far neither Anthropic nor Google have resources to do that, rather they employ millions of fine-tuning samples. And I heart those companies have lots of money. It is true that modern LLM-s are trained to do basic chain-of-thoughts/agentic loops at the very begginning of fine-tuning (i.e. after pre-training), but it should be noted that LLM can do implicit chain of thought and code writing BEFORE any fine-tuning. Just the base model can do that, but the format of input and output does not correspond to what humans and harness expect. And that's basically how the chain of thoughts was discovered: researchers asked LLM to solve some task step by step — and it did. Nobody trained LLM to do that, it just reproduced some patterns from pre-training sets. And then researches started training LLM-s to specifically optimize agentic loops. > I don't know what to tell ya, it's how the LLM sausage is made. Even small Phi-4 was pre-trained on only 40% synthetic data, despite Phi-1 employing 99%+ synthetic data. Once again, you should split pre-training and post-training. On modern super-large LLM-s the large corpus of agentic loops for fine-tuning is indeed generated via external expert agentic loops, but it never becomes 100% as the model collapse is real and well known. Just in case the wording "model collapse" is not clear: the model starts using extremely limited set of tools to solve every task, even when much more efficient tools are available. I can see the tendency for model collapse on Grok 4.7 and Sonnet 5.5 I often use, and their engineers definitely partially counteracted this tendency. >I usually see this in people who are struggling to downplay LLM capabilities, and their strategy is to pretend that everything LLMs are good at was trivially accessible in the training data all along. I tried feeding non-canonical Tarjan bridge-finding implementation into AI approx year ago, and it went totally crazy: it says the implementation is incorrect, then traces it via supposed counter-example and finds it correct, then tries to give new explanation and once again suggests the implementation is bugged... The fact we put lots of crutches beneath the same pattern-matcher does not make it a completely different mechanism. Most people never leave their sit during the AI ride so AI drives them through the pre-defined happy path. But once you try to deliberately leave this road, LLM-s often mark the code "wrong/unoptimal/poorly formatted". That's particularly a reason why older agents used to agressively introduce completely unrelated refactoring/formatting changes — because they just did not like how many spaces you've used in your code — and modern LLM-s still suffer from this problem, but their harness and agentic loops usually hide at least part of those meaningless changes. The phenomena is long-known, LLM-s strongly prefer their own ideomatic code:  https://openreview.net/forum?id=4NJBV6Wp0h  >I said "LLMs are capable of learning and extrapolating knowledge to new problems". You can throw a novel problem at an LLM and you'll get a novel solution. My experience is quite the opposite: I give a novel problem and LLM suggests 10-years old solution using libraries that are long deprecated. My whole life's hobby is about finding rare stuff, and I have very broad experience in this area. I particularly like LLM-s for finding some rare old thing I've never heard about, but in terms of making up something totally novel LLM-s totally sucks. Arguably, an ant is more intelligent when dealing with novel conditions than the most sophisticated modern LLM is.

I think the article is insightful. I want to contribute my perspective: 1. when an AI starts working on a task, it is within a human context, someone pays and decides to assign that work to AI 2. while it performs work on the task it continuously needs to interact with the context in order to act and observe the feedback 3. at the end of work, the outcomes remain in context, including gains, losses, costs, risks and liability. So AI is great but can't do the beginning, middle and end of a task. They belong to context, which is us, the AI users. Context is maximally distributed, every human, team, or company that uses AI is a context, they are relational and indexical. You can't have my context, for example - you can't eat for me, or learn for me. Some things must loop back. Especially consequences of AI work. That is irreducible, AI can't improve to grow a skin like us. Its own skin is user base gain/loss, competition with other AI providers and dancing for investors. Every AI usage context is not theirs and they can't own it. What happens to companies is that their investors expect AI usage already, their competitors use it to compete with them and fast follow, and customers use AI agents to arbitrate their buying opportunities. So even if they did nothing AI related they find themselves in a new world where. 1. anything visible can be easily imitated - code, text, media, and AI agents - I call it the fast follow effect 2. any apparent arbitrage opportunity will be quickly crowded by fast followers removing profit from it 3. AI it self is competitive and the whole stack is fungible - models, harnesses, tools, they can all be replaced easily, what matters more is the project context data which is usually a git backed folder on local disk So my theory is that AI won't make anyone "rich". Instead we have a musical chairs moment. AI removes distinctiveness from everyone of us. Every time I use AI for myself it is just great and amazing. When others use it, they make our own work seem little and not as impressive. Companies are caught in a Red Queen effect, have to work harder just to stay in place. And here I find the answer to what will we do with all our free time - compete, run for our own musical chair. We need to find our own niches again, they are now under rapid change. We will invest as much energy as needed to do it, we are ready to pay a lot of effort to differentiate back. But we can't predict it just as you can't predict where the ball in a football match will go 1 minute later, it depends on what every other player is doing.

I think your response misses pretty important distinctions between art and practical pursuits. People get upset when other people use AI in the arts because the point is largely  human expression . Technical virtuosity isn't even necessarily the most important thing in art (just look at modern art and how common the philistine refrain of "my kid could do that" is). Art doesn't serve a utilitarian function. Using AI for it largely misses the point, and I think that's what people get upset about. It's like showing up to play tag and saying "actually I'm going to play hide and seek instead" you aren't following the established social norms of the game. Contests, in general, always ways have restrictions around them, because they are meant to test particular human feats. I'm sure plenty of future contests will have rules against AI just as today plenty of contests arbitrarily limit technologies for the good of the competition (e.g. no doping in sports). To respond to this situation by emphasizing the utilitarian function and value of AI is to completely miss the point.
